p.x:
just watched the original ghostbusters for the first time, scattered thoughts

 - 1984 in NYC, no asians or latinos, handful of black characters, some background hasidic jews

 - i continue to wonder if characters make more eye contact in older movies, there's a bunch of subtle-for-2026 eye contact stuff going on that i feel like just used to be normal and has mostly disappeared? 

 - bill murray's character is weirder than i expected, felt like he was possibly ad libbing in a few places? does some stuff that would be somewhere between sexual harassment and sexual assault now which is interesting

 - don't see slime like this anymore. there was a period where pop culture was obsessed with slime that just totally disappeared like it never happened

 - sigourney weaver is amazingly charming, does a lot with just a few smiles, but also her character is super passive and pretty much just a trophy, i guess it makes sense why people rebelled so hard against this sort of thing

 - feels like guys like dan aykroyd don't exist anymore. don't think we know how to make guys like that anymore. i hope that's not true but 42 years is a long time for culture to shift

 - there's a moment where they casually quote revelations and suggest that the climax of the movie is judgment day and another moment where a bishop or something casually swings by to advise the mayor. there is this like casual background air of christianity that i'm not sure exists anymore

 - how did i not know that one of the lines of the ghostbusters theme is "bustin' makes me feel good"???

p.x:
When I was in the navy, I invented a game called "talking" that played off what I understood as a fundamental mechanism of human cognition.

A player starts with a random word. The other responds with a word that is not related in any way to the previous. They continue back and forth in this way, maintaining eye contact. If a player uses the environment or a symantic connection from any words used prior to generate their word, the other can call them out and win.

This is extremely difficult due to how we optimize conversation for contextual relevance.

I came up with this before the existence of transformers, and somehow didn't think about it until now. 

Bing is extremely good at this, which blows my mind,
but will hallucinate that it won and end the conversation before you can argue with it. An effective strategy.

p.x:
The world changed last week—Opus 4.5 is the best coding model I’ve ever used.

It can keep coding and coding autonomously without tripping over itself—and it marks a completely new horizon for the craft of programming. The dream is here: You can write English, and make software.

So I invited Paul Ford on to @every’s AI and I to talk about it. Paul is the co-founder of @aboard and also prolific writer. He authored one of my favorite pieces of technology writing What Is Code?—so he’s the perfect person to unpack it with me.

We talk about the wonder—and genuine unease—that comes with using tools this powerful. We get into what people who love technology should care about as the ground under us shifts faster than we can imagine:

- Why Opus 4.5 is such a significant leap and what it means
- How we’ve both been using it for the last week to build more things more quickly than we thought was possible
- What it feels like when the lines between the categories —“I'm a frontend engineer,” “I'm a designer”—that used to define your identity start to blur
- What this actually means for programming and the craft of code
- What the risks of this are, and what the transition to an economy where code is cheap will be like

This is a must-watch for anyone who cares about coding in the AI era.
